item.title: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
item.abstract: November 10, 2026 Research Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri Read the technical paper How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. How we verified Signal AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties – such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised – down to the exact code running on devices. Because real-world vulnerabilities often hide in the gap between design and implementation, bridging this gap makes these proofs vastly more complex. Even at this complexity, our verification process took just four weeks – a task that historically takes expert teams years – proving that Signal's core cryptographic code delivers the security protections our experts specified. To confirm that AlphaProof Code can tell correct code from buggy code, we reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code. In both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure. In AlphaProof Code, AI agents help users write a specification, then autonomously prove that the implementation meets it. Every proof is checked by Lean to verify the agents' work. While prior formal verification focused on smaller portions of the code, Google DeepMind's approach enables significant expansion,” said Ehren Kret, Chief Technology Officer of Signal. “Using AI agents to translate live code into valid Lean theorems is a major breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code's privacy guarantees. Ehren Kret Chief Technology Officer of Signal While prior formal verification work has necessarily focused on smaller scopes, this new approach enables a significant expansion. Traditionally, verifying that production code strictly matches its cryptographic design required extensive manual effort, making the use of AI agents to automatically translate live code into valid Lean theorems a great breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, having the core Signal protocol rigorously verified with automated theorem proving gives us even greater confidence that our code delivers on its privacy guarantees. The future of security Achieving this long-standing challenge demonstrates how AI can bring elite security assurance to businesses, governments, and critical infrastructure, helping defend against agent-driven cyber threats. Verifying Signal's core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software. Scaling these techniques requires continued research. Paired with automated defense agents like CodeMender , formal verification can help counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats to create software with mathematical proof that its protections work. We are open-sourcing our formal verification artifacts for community use. Read the technical paper below. We thank Eric Wieser for help with open-sourcing our code, Owen Jones for program management support, and Martín Abadi, Christopher Henson, Katerina Hristova, Henryk Michalewski, Jonathan Protzenko and George Tsoukalas for helpful discussions. We thank Signal's Rolfe Schmidt, Michael Rosenberg, and Ehren Kret for their feedback on our methodology. item.title: Gemini 4 Carbon is now available
item.abstract: Gemini 4 Carbon is now available Nov 10, 2026 | Developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers can now try our latest frontier model. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X In this article Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning. Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops. Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model. To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change. Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , the Gemini app , and AI Mode in Search . Higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. It follows strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports. Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark that tests a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows. Carbon ranks #2 while being more than 6X lower in average cost per task compared to the top performing model. Using Google Antigravity’s new /swarm feature, a team of Gemini 4 Carbon agents turned historical photos and engineering plates into an interactive Three.js 3D exhibition of the Eiffel Tower's 1887–1889 construction from a single prompt. With seven public City Council planning PDFs (206 extracted engineering drawing views) and a single prompt, a multi-agent Carbon team using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature built an interactive 906K-triangle Three.js reconstruction of Google’s Platform 37 office across 10 overnight loops. In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Carbon built an interactive multiscale textile visualizer based on an academic paper, modeling a virtual-fiber finite element framework with interactive 3D yarn meshes, 110-fiber polar tracking, and dynamic stress-strain curves with minimal prompting. In pre-release evaluations, Carbon matched the performance of the best model tested on deep financial research on Hebbia’s E2E Financial Agentic evaluation, and ranked at the top out of 23 frontier model configurations on Balyasny Asset Management’s General Financial Intelligence benchmark, spanning legal expertise, agentic tool use and execution, coding and data engineering, and perception and context understanding. Improved agentic coding, full stack development, and 3D and UI design Carbon performs exceptionally well on engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration like multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. For web app development, it runs build-and-verify loops, recovers from errors, and checks both its code and the rendered UI to produce complete, working applications. Stronger visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail also carry over to 3D game development and creative coding. Using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature, Carbon built an open-world 3D game where you explore Google’s Mountain View campus as a pelican riding a GBike — coordinating subagents to model 3D assets in Blender from Omni and Nano Banana references, build the browser game in Three.js with WebGL shaders, and pair procedural Web Audio sound effects with Lyria music. Try the live app . Paired with improved front end taste and motion design skills in Google Antigravity, Carbon reimagined the Google Merchandise Store in two prompts, proposing five art direction concepts and generating all-new product imagery with Nano Banana 2.1. Try the live app and Gemini front end design skill . Starting from a video reference generated with Gemini Omni in Google Antigravity, built a cinematic multi-shot underwater Atlantis scene. The pipeline modeled procedural ruins, volumetric caustic lighting, and water simulation in Blender before converting the full environment to Three.js for real-time browser rendering. Using a multi-agent loop in Google Antigravity, Carbon reconstructed a playable c. 1780 Stein-Schule fortepiano with 61-key escapement physics from CAD drawings and X-ray radiographs and placed it in a 3D model of the Royal Conservatory of Music's Koerner Hall in Toronto with seat-specific spatial acoustics. Try the live app . Frontier cybersecurity capabilities Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber delivers our strongest cybersecurity capabilities to date, giving security teams the end-to-end intelligence they need in protecting critical software. When accessed through the Fairwind Program, Carbon leads on key benchmarks across finding (SEC-bench Pro), exploiting (ExploitGym), and patching (CWE-bench v1) vulnerabilities: inspecting software, tracing how flaws can be chained together across systems, and generating verified root-cause patches. Early testers inside and outside of Google are already seeing strong results with Carbon for cyber in practice. In Project Fortify , Google’s autonomous system spanning scanning, triage, and remediation, Carbon hit 100% recall on scanning and 95% precision on triage, on our internal benchmark. On Open Source code repository testing we see an over 25% relative improvement on Argon's already strong recall rate, surfacing previously undetected, real-world logic flaws. Bringing these gains across Google, one of the world’s largest users of open-source software, helps secure both our own systems and the broader ecosystem. Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team recently used Carbon to prove that two bugs in a popular open-source software were in fact exploitable vulnerabilities, comparable in severity to the recent PHP2Shell exploit . By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch. Details will be shared after the responsible disclosure process completes.

item.title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
item.abstract: Microsoft researchers have discovered “Lazarus,” a backdoor technique that can reprogram dormant neurons in an AI model, causing an otherwise normal AI agent to execute malicious commands when a hidden trigger appears. The threat is especially serious for AI agents with tool or terminal access. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, steal secrets, or execute destructive commands while still passing standard safety evaluations. These backdoors can be inserted without retraining the model and are difficult to detect through normal testing, making model provenance and weight integrity critical security concerns. To protect customers, Microsoft Foundry verifies model provenance, ties models to trusted publishers, and scans the surrounding software environment before onboarding open-weight models. Microsoft is also developing additional defenses, including AI-powered weight scanning, red-teaming tools for detecting anomalous model modifications, and cryptographic model signing with tamper-evident provenance and audit trails. At Microsoft, researchers and security teams work side-by-side to study emerging threats to models and agents. Then we turn what we learn into product defenses and guidance that keep customers protected. More broadly, Lazarus is an example of a practice that should become routine: AI agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them. Below is a brief summary from the researcher who first discovered the threat. We find (opens in new tab) that weight-reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM, is enough to backdoor an agent built on it, and requires no training. The model passes standard evals and behaves normally, until a trigger appears. The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent—in the middle of an ordinary task—emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code. The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it. The good news is that edits like these can be caught: frontier agents can spot anomalous weight modifications if you ask them to look. But no scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe. Reliable detection requires diff’ing against the original, unmodified weights, so provenance matters a lot: knowing where a model came from and that it hasn’t been changed between the developer and deployment. Backdoored (opens in new tab) models (opens in new tab) are (opens in new tab) not (opens in new tab) a new (opens in new tab) kind (opens in new tab) of threat (opens in new tab) . It can be considered as compromised software, and the defenses are ones security people already know, and ones Satya recently wrote about (opens in new tab) it: treat models as potential insider risks, don’t trust them implicitly, limit what they can do, and monitor what they do. Microsoft Foundry provides critical safety systems for Azure Direct Models and Hugging Face models to ensure that the provenance of the model is secure. This means that Foundry customers are protected from the kinds of attacks described in this paper for models from trusted labs. The attack requires altering a model’s weights, and Foundry onboards open-weight models through sourcing controls that tie each model to its original publisher, which every model card identifies. Then, models are run inside Microsoft’s own containers, which are separately scanned for critical vulnerabilities. These controls cover where a model came from and the software around it. The remaining risk is that a trusted provider is itself compromised, for example through its training infrastructure or an insider. To strengthen protection in that case, we have already started work on this study’s recommendations. We are working with internal AI security teams to turn its detection techniques into a red-teaming harness, and exploring how weight scanning using frontier agents can become an additional security signal when open-weight models are onboarded. Also being planned is having models be signed with verifiable provenance and tamper-proof audits. Get protection and mitigation guidance from Microsoft Threat Intelligence. (opens in new tab) Here is what we suggest as a starting point: This started back in March as a quick experiment: I asked Claude Code with Opus 4.5 to backdoor a model by hardwiring a few activations without training. And it did. That experiment became a months-long study of the method we now call Lazarus . Here is what we learned: This is a simplified depiction of how Lazarus works. item.title: Mitra-v2: Scaling synthetic pretraining for tabular foundation models
item.abstract: Much of the data that businesses run on lives in tables: the rows might represent customers, transactions, or interactions, and their “attributes” are listed in the columns. Predicting missing attributes — such as likelihood of customer retention or how much demand to expect next week — is one of the most common machine learning tasks in industry. The standard tools for this job, such as gradient-boosted decision trees, produce models tailored to specific tables. Every new table means choosing an algorithm, engineering features, tuning hyperparameters, and setting up a processing pipeline. Tabular foundation models promise to end that cycle: one pretrained model reads the labeled rows of a previously unseen table and predicts the rest, with no training run in-between. Last year we introduced Mitra, a tabular foundation model pretrained entirely on synthetic tables. It worked well on small and mid-sized tables but ran out of room on large ones, wide ones, and problems with many classes. Today we're introducing Mitra-v2, the second generation of the model, for both classification and regression. We describe it in a technical report, and we've released versions fine-tuned for both classification and regression, along with the inference and fine-tuning code, under the Apache-2.0 license on Hugging Face. Amazon Connect Customer, which provides agentic-AI systems for core business functions, led the effort. Amazon Connect Customer is adopting Mitra-v2 for prediction on structured business and customer-experience data, such as estimating how likely a business-relevant event is to occur given a customer's interaction history and operational context. On TabArena, a public benchmark of 51 real-world datasets, Mitra-v2 leads the single-model field. It produces a better result than Mitra-v1 on 32 of the 33 datasets where both models run natively, and it completes all 51 datasets within the benchmark's one-hour budget, which Mitra-v1 failed to do on more than a third of them. On ScoringBench, a public benchmark for regression models that predict a range of likely outcomes rather than a single number, fine-tuned Mitra-v2 ranks first. Synthetic pretraining A large language model is pretrained on huge volumes of data, so when you give it a few examples in a prompt, it can generalize from them with no additional training. Tabular foundation models work the same way. We pretrain Mitra-v2 on millions of synthetic prediction problems, and at deployment time the labeled rows of a real table serve as the examples. The model reads them and predicts the unlabeled rows, a technique called in-context learning. Every pretraining table is synthetic: we use no real data, and in particular, no customer data. The model learns general principles about how columns relate to one another rather than the contents of any real dataset. The lesson of the original Mitra was that the quality and diversity of those synthetic tables are central to how well the model generalizes. Mitra-v2 takes that lesson further. The architecture is unchanged: a Transformer that attends both across the rows of a table and across its columns. What has changed is the size of the examples the model sees during pretraining. Mitra-v2 is pretrained on tables with 10 times as many rows and roughly three times as many columns as those used to train Mitra-v1, so it has seen tables the size of the ones businesses actually use. We also added a new family of synthetic tables. To train the original Mitra, we generated tables from structural causal models (SCMs), which are graphs of cause-and-effect relationships between columns, and from tree-based models like the ones data scientists fit in practice. Mitra-v2's new hybrid SCM prior builds a single causal graph in which each relationship can be a small neural network, a decision tree, a smooth function drawn from a Gaussian process, or a time-dependent autoregressive process, so one synthetic table can carry the mix of relationships found in real tables. A new hybrid optimizer keeps training stable across this wider range. At deployment time, two lightweight wrappers extend the model beyond its pretraining limits. For very wide tables, we use singular-value decomposition to produce a new table that fits in the allotted space, populated with synthetic values that capture most of the variance in the original data. Mitra-v2’s output layer has only 10 nodes, corresponding to 10 classes, so for tasks with more classes than that, we send each node’s output toa a hierarchical tree, which further refines the classification. By default, Mitra-v2 is briefly, automatically fine-tuned on each new table it sees, producing eight copies whose predictions are averaged, a standard technique called bagging. So it isn't quite a zero-shot model. The adaptation adds some computational overhead, but in return, it delivers higher accuracy and gives customers additional options. Results We evaluated Mitra-v2 on TabArena, a living benchmark maintained by an independent academic team. TabArena ranks methods by Elo, the rating system used in chess, here computed from head-to-head wins across datasets under a fixed one-hour budget. Mitra-v2 leads the single-model field, as shown below, with large gains over Mitra-v1 on both classification and regression. It also ranks among the leading methods on the independent TALENT benchmark of roughly 300 datasets, where it's strongest on classification tasks with more than 10 classes. Full results, including per-dataset comparisons, are in the technical report. For regression, Mitra-v2 predicts a full range of likely values for each row rather than a single number, so users get prediction intervals along with the point estimate. That’s the approach that ScoringBench evaluates, rewarding forecasts that are both accurate and well calibrated. On the ScoringBench leaderboard, fine-tuned Mitra-v2 again ranks first. Mitra-v2 shows that a tabular foundation model can make substantial gains by widening the diversity and range of its synthetic pretraining, without a deeper network. We expect richer synthetic priors and adaptive mixtures to push this further. The fine-tuned classification and regression models and code are open on Hugging Face and ready to use, and we invite researchers and practitioners to try Mitra-v2 on their own tables. item.title: Agent Substrate: Advancing Kubernetes for Agents at Scale
item.abstract: AI agents spend most of their time idle, waiting on a human prompt, a tool result or a model response. Kubernetes wasn’t built for that. Running one Pod per session holds memory for sessions that aren’t doing anything, and deleting Pods between turns pays a multi-second cold start every time and loses the agent’s state. RL post-training hits the same wall. Agent Substrate, now donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox, is an open-source, security-hardened, zero-trust runtime for sandboxed agents, engineered to safely run millions of agents and tools with 10x higher density than standard containers. It multiplexes many sessions over a small pool of worker Pods. Idle sessions are checkpointed, memory and filesystem included, and restored onto whichever worker is free when the next request arrives. As agentic infrastructure fragments into proprietary runtimes that bypass Kubernetes, NVIDIA is contributing upstream to keep this work open. This post covers which workloads suit Agent Substrate, what is being built upstream, and how the project works with KAI Scheduler and NVIDIA Dynamo components in the DSX AI Factory Platform . The shape of an agent workload Traditional web services run as a relatively small number of long-lived instances. Agents follow a different pattern: they wake up and take one step, running a shell command, editing a file, calling a test suite or calling an LLM. Then they wait, sometimes for milliseconds and sometimes for minutes, before the next step. The agent’s state (its filesystem, its processes, its working directory) has to continue between steps. Kubernetes struggles because spinning up a compute Pod for an agent means a trip through the API server, admission, etcd, the scheduler, the kubelet, image pulls and network setup. That takes seconds, which is fine for a service that runs for weeks. It’s far too slow for a sandbox that must appear, run a 10 ms bash command and get out of the way, hundreds of times per second. This leaves platform teams with two suboptimal choices: either keep one Pod warm per agent and pay for compute that is idle almost all the time, or create Pods on demand and pay a cold start penalty on every step. How Agent Substrate works Agent Substrate uses Kubernetes for running a pool of ready pods. It creates a separate control plane that maps a large set of actors (agents and their environments) onto that smaller pool of workers. When an actor goes idle, it is snapshotted out of its sandbox (gVisor or a microVM) and its worker is freed. When the actor is called again, it is restored into whichever worker is free, with its memory and filesystem state intact. Waking an actor doesn’t require a new trip through the API server, scheduler or kubelet. Agent Substrate restores the actor onto an existing worker instead. The worker pods are still ordinary Kubernetes Pods, so cluster scheduling, quotas and placement policies still apply as we describe later. The use cases driving demand We see three kinds of workload driving demand for Agent Substrate: Coding assistants and agent serving: A coding agent alternates between LLM calls and work in its own environment: cloning a repository, editing files, running builds and tests. Users expect the environment to persist between turns and to respond immediately. A platform serving thousands of these sessions can’t afford a dedicated warm sandbox for each one. Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training with agentic environments: RL with verifiable rewards runs GPU trainers and generation servers alongside a fleet of CPU-heavy environments (code sandboxes, compilers, browsers, simulators) that execute actions and check results. Sandbox demand arrives in bursts as rollout batches dispatch actions. A training run can grow from a few hundred sandboxes in early experiments to many hundreds of thousands in production. The slowest environment determines when the trainer gets its next batch, so cold starts on that path leave GPUs idle. GPU sandboxes for research: A researcher’s coding agent needs a GPU, not to serve a model but to compile CUDA code, benchmark a kernel or run a numerical calculation. It launches a GPU sandbox on a shared cluster, runs the job and deletes the sandbox. Supporting this across an organization requires many short-lived, isolated GPU sandboxes that start quickly and share a limited pool of GPUs fairly. Upstream work: What’s landed and what’s next Each contribution below started from one of those use cases. All of this work is public in the Agent Substrate repository : When every worker is busy, the next request waits instead of failing: In an oversubscribed system, such as a coding-assistant platform at peak or an RL rollout burst, a user’s next turn can arrive while every worker is busy. Agent Substrate used to return an error immediately, even though another actor would usually free a worker a moment later. Request parking in the Agent Substrate router ( #221 ) holds the request and retries the resume until a worker frees up, with a bounded wait and a cap on how many requests can wait at once. A follow-up ( #1229 ) makes sure requests to already-running actors never get stuck in that line. Giving agents a GPU inside their sandbox: The research GPU sandbox described above, along with GPU-backed RL environments such as simulators. We are working on device-pluggability that adds device support on Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA). Device vendors plug in their devices through a profile, each container in a sandbox requests only the devices it needs ( #752 ), and the same model works for both gVisor and microVM sandboxes. NVIDIA GPUs will be the first supported device. One container can’t starve or kill its neighbors: An agent sandbox often runs the agent’s workload next to helper containers for logging, proxying or metrics. Some of those may be untrusted. A runaway container shouldn’t consume the whole sandbox’s memory and take the agent down with it. Per-container CPU and memory limits for microVM sandboxes ( #859 ) addresses that issue. A container that exceeds its memory limit is stopped on its own, and the rest of the sandbox keeps running. Preserving GPU sandboxes across suspend and resume When an agent pauses to wait for human review, its sandbox should release the GPU and resume later with its compiled artifacts and loaded data still in place. Supporting that requires saving and restoring both the agent’s state and the GPU state. Restoring GPU state introduces hardware compatibility constraints. A GPU checkpoint can usually be restored only onto the same GPU model, and sometimes only with the same driver version. Agent Substrate proposes a design to address this. Device vendors describe how to pause their devices safely and which device properties a snapshot depends on. Agent Substrate records those properties with each snapshot and restores the sandbox on a matching device, or falls back to a clean cold start if none is available. The design is vendor-neutral and builds on DRA. NVIDIA GPUs are the first target; the design can be extended to other hardware types. NVIDIA Dynamo: Connecting the agent loop to the inference loop Agent Substrate manages where agents act; inference runtimes manage where they think. Both face a similar efficiency challenge: keeping idle sandboxes warm wastes CPU and memory, while rebuilding model context on repeated model calls wastes GPU cycles. Scaling each layer independently improves utilization. Coordinating them can also reduce latency and preserve reusable context as agents move between tool execution and model calls. NVIDIA Dynamo , the open-source distributed inference framework, provides that coordination. Agent Substrate activates, suspends and restores stateful agent environments across a pool of warm sandbox workers. Dynamo orchestrates inference across GPU workers. The Dynamo router sits between them and connects what the agent is doing with what is happening on the GPUs.

item.title: MBZUAI’s IFM Releases PAN 2, an Open 29B World Model for Physical AI
item.abstract: The Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) at MBZUAI released PAN 2 , an open world model for physical intelligence. The PAN 2 world model takes a scene and a text action and simulates the outcome as video. IFM announced it on X on November 10, 2026. Weights, training code and inference code ship under Apache 2.0 . For robotics and agent developers, the pitch is simple: test a plan in simulation before acting on it. PAN 2 is a general-purpose world model from IFM that simulates how a scene changes after an action. It follows the Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture from IFM’s Critique of World Models paper. It succeeds PAN , released in November 2025. The goal is simulative reasoning . An agent proposes plans, PAN 2 simulates each one, and the agent acts on the best. PAN 2 splits simulation into 2 kinds of reasoning : IFM’s ablation shows the LLM matters. With no conceptual reasoning, full-plan completion drops from 34.0% to 0.0%. Step completion falls from 75.1% to 8.7%. A format-only rewrite recovers part of the gap, reaching 27.8% full-plan completion. IFM also dropped gameplay, animation and simulation footage after early training. A 9B test model trained without it won 58% of blinded votes. All numbers below are self-reported by IFM. Its own test suite covers 6 capabilities across 300 single-action cases, plus 100 multi-step tasks. *Scores from IFM’s PAN 2 model card , run by IFM. The blog reports different Cosmos 3 Super and LTX-2.5 plan scores. PAN 2 supports text-to-video and image-to-video. You can run it through Hugging Face Diffusers , vLLM , FastVideo or the repo’s generate.py . The default sampler uses 50 steps, flow shift 9 and guidance 2.5. item.title: Zyphra Releases ZONOS3-Mini: Open-Source TTS With 100M Active Parameters
item.abstract: Zyphra has released ZONOS3-Mini , an open-source text-to-speech model built for real-time use on local devices. The ZONOS3-Mini text-to-speech model is a sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) with 800M total and 100M active parameters. It supports zero-shot voice cloning and word-level delivery control. Weights ship under Apache 2.0. For AI devs, size is the key point. It runs in a browser tab, on a laptop or on a server GPU. ZONOS3-Mini is a compact zero-shot voice-cloning TTS model from Zyphra that runs in real time on-device. Zyphra trained it on 112 NVIDIA H100s in 2.5 days. It follows ZONOS2 , which used 8B parameters and an 86 Hz codec. That size limited where ZONOS2 could be deployed. Zyphra changed 3 layers of the stack : Identity controls cover age, gender, accent and voice texture through speaker embedding vectors and accent task vectors. Delivery controls cover pace, emotion, projection and liveliness through activation steering. Learned alignment heads let steering apply to specific words during streaming. A separate edit model, based on a VoiceCraft recipe, can modify sentences after generation. Zyphra evaluated the model on its new ZTTS2-Eval benchmark. It covers 35 languages of clean read speech and 20 languages of in-the-wild recordings. A Capability Index uses item response theory over 420 items. ZONOS3-Mini in speaker-embedding mode scores 66.2 on that index. Fish Audio S2 Pro scores 61.7 and MOSS-TTS v1.5 scores 60.2. On the clean set, ZONOS3-Mini posts 7.79 WER and 83.4 speaker similarity. There are caveats. Zyphra built and ran the benchmark. Reference-clip mode scores only 44.7 on the index. item.title: Start and Restore GPU Workloads in Seconds with NVIDIA Snapshot
item.abstract: NVIDIA Snapshot , a new open-source component of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , makes initialized GPU workloads reusable across inference replicas—speeding startup and recovery. When inference demand spikes or a replica fails, available GPUs don’t translate immediately into serving capacity. Initializing an LLM workload—a process known as a cold start—can take minutes, delaying scaling and recovery. Snapshot is a checkpoint and restore system for GPU workloads on Kubernetes. It captures a fully initialized workload—including CPU and GPU memory—and restores that state on compatible infrastructure, bringing inference capacity online in seconds instead of minutes. Figure 1 shows the startup sequence. Snapshot skips repeated workload initialization; infrastructure provisioning and container image loading remain outside the measured restore path. Figure 1. Cold-start sequence: provision the machine, load the container image, start the inference engine, load model weights into GPU memory, compile with torch.compile, and capture NVIDIA CUDA graphs This post explains how Snapshot checkpoints and restores GPU workloads, how platform teams can integrate it, and how restore times compare with cold starts across three inference engines. Snapshot for AI factory operations Originally developed for NVIDIA Dynamo inference workers, Snapshot provides checkpoint and restore capabilities that other inference engines, schedulers, controllers, and platforms can integrate. Snapshot provides two operations for GPU Pods: Checkpoint : Once a workload is fully initialized, capture its CPU and GPU memory as a portable artifact. Restore : Start a new Pod from that artifact on any node with the same GPU model and driver. The process continues from where it was checkpointed, so weight loading, compilation, and graph capture are skipped. Both operations use Kubernetes custom resources. To checkpoint a Pod that is already running, create a PodSnapshot that names it. To start a Pod from a template and checkpoint it as soon as it is ready, create a SnapshotJob instead. To restore, add the annotation nvidia.com/restore-from to a new Pod, naming the PodSnapshot to restore from. The workload only needs a small handshake to pause before the checkpoint and resume after the restore. The repository has ready-made examples for vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM . Snapshot can checkpoint and restore compatible workloads that span multiple GPUs on a single node as a single checkpoint artifact across ranks. This supports fast startup for large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models using parallelism strategies such as tensor parallelism (TP), data and expert parallelism (DEP), and decode context parallelism (DCP). Workloads must meet Snapshot’s checkpoint/restore and runtime compatibility requirements . See the example configurations . Benchmarks Design partners have also evaluated Snapshot on their own workloads: Crusoe , an upstream contributor to Snapshot, reduced GLM-5.3 Pod readiness time from roughly 8 minutes to 31 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300. Saturn Cloud , a token factory platform, benchmarked NVIDIA Snapshot for scale-from-zero inference, cutting vLLM startup from 2–8.5 minutes to 6–34 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300 . The following benchmarks show how Snapshot accelerates inference startup across vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM (TRT-LLM)—with models from 600 million parameters to mixture-of-experts (MoE) models with 1 TB checkpoints on 8 GPUs. Across all tested configurations, Snapshot brings a replica back in under 45 seconds, 8x to 36x faster than a cold start. Methodology Each configuration was tested using two strategies on the same hardware and software stack: Cold start: The workload starts from scratch. The clock runs from process launch until engine initialization returns, before inference. The measurement is divided into four phases (Table 2): Startup: Starting the engine and worker processes, importing Python libraries, and setting up communication between GPUs. Some just-in-time (JIT) kernel compilation also happens here. Model load: Reading the model weights and constructing the model’s tensors, including any engine-specific conversion or repacking done while loading. Initialization: Preparing the loaded model to serve: memory profiling, allocating the key-value (KV) cache and runtime buffers, and other kernel and runtime preparation. Compilation, autotuning, and graph capture: Compiling kernels (for example, with torch.compile ), autotuning them for the GPU, and capturing CUDA graphs. Snapshot: The workload is restored from its checkpoint. The clock runs from the moment Snapshot is asked to restore until the workload is serving again. The measurement is divided into four stages (Table 3): Agent setup: The Snapshot agent on the node locates the checkpoint artifact and prepares the target Pod and GPUs. Checkpoint/Restore in Userspace (CRIU) restore: CRIU, the standard Linux tool for checkpointing processes, reads the process image from storage into host memory. Speed is set mostly by the storage backend. CUDA restore: Copying GPU state back into GPU memory. Wake/remap: Adapting the process to the new node and waking the engine. Both measurements exclude pulling the container image and setting up the container runtime. The KV cache release is triggered before every checkpoint, so it is not part of the artifact. Table 1 also reports checkpoint time and size: how long it takes to capture a fully initialized replica and how much storage the stored artifact requires. This is a one-time cost per model and configuration. Setup GPU: NVIDIA B200 NVIDIA driver: 615.71.09 Storage backend: VAST (NFS) Inference engines: vLLM 0.31.0 SGLang 0.5.21 TensorRT LLM 1.3.0 Results The benchmarks show four main findings. Restore times stayed under 43 seconds: Across all tested configurations, Snapshot restored replicas in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds—8x to 36x faster than cold start. The largest MoE models, with checkpoints of about 600 GB to 1 TB across eight GPUs, restored in under 43 seconds compared with cold-start times of 6 to 19 minutes. Restoring skips more than weight loading: Cold-start time includes loading weights, compiling and autotuning kernels, and capturing CUDA graphs. Snapshot restores the initialized workload, skipping these repeated steps. Checkpointing pays off with the first restored replica: In every tested configuration, checkpoint time plus restore time was shorter than a single cold start. Checkpoint creation took 15 seconds to 5.5 minutes, depending on the model and configuration. Moving GPU state dominates large restores: For the eight-GPU MoE configurations, restoring GPU state took 18 to 29 seconds. Restoring CPU process state with CRIU took 4.2 to 10.8 seconds. Figures 2 to 4 compare cold-start and Snapshot restore times for vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT LLM across the tested models and parallelism configurations. Table 1 provides the data for every configuration, including checkpoint time and size. All times are in seconds. In the figures and tables, TEP8 denotes tensor and expert parallelism across eight GPUs . Figure 2. vLLM: Cold start compared with Snapshot for every model and parallelism tested. Snapshot brings each replica up in 4.7 to 39.6 seconds Figure 3. SGLang: Cold start compared with Snapshot for every model and parallelism tested. Snapshot brings each replica up in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds Figure 4. TensorRT LLM (TRT-LLM): Cold start compared with Snapshot for every model and parallelism tested. item.title: DeepMind reveals Gemini Robotics 2.5 and open safety benchmark "ASIMOV-jailbreak"
item.abstract: Google DeepMind has revealed a new generation of the AI-powered Gemini Robotics platform. In the 2.5 release, Google says its robotic AI is getting tantalizingly close to completing real-world tasks as well as humans do. In fact, some Gemini robots were able to get actual work done in Mercedes-Benz factories, and the team is preparing for a day when robots operate alongside humans with an open source safety benchmark. DeepMind's physical AI platform has several computational layers between user input and robotic action. There's the vision-language model piece, which is Gemini Embodied Reasoning. Essentially, it takes your instructions and uses live video to plan how the robot can accomplish the task. The other main component is the vision-language-action (VLA) that actually generates robot actions, like moving an actuator—that's Gemini Robotics, which has been bumped to version 2.5. DeepMind says that Gemini Robotics 2.5 is much better at tasks that require a high degree of dexterity. The model was evaluated across more than 200 activities, including serving food with tongs and using a pipette, as you would see in a laboratory. Google also showed that Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot with Gemini Robotics 2.5 can now tie a bow with its five-fingered hands, a notable feat, because deformable objects (like ribbon) are notoriously difficult for robots to manipulate.

item.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
item.abstract: Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here’s the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s that transcript —Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”. The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample: What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right? That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort. It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways. item.title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
item.abstract: research area Methods and Algorithms , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing Workshop at NeurIPS content type paper published November 2026 Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval Authors William L. Tong†**, Aryo Lotfi, Emmanuel Abbe, Josh Susskind, Cengiz Pehlevan†, Eran Malach View publication Copy Bibtex This paper was accepted at the Workshop on Personalized, Aligned, Long-term Memory for AI Systems (PALM) at NeurIPS 2026. State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded contexts, limiting their utility for long-horizon domains. To address this issue, we propose weighted state souping, a simple method that learns query-dependent weights for composing cached states. The resulting models improve long-context performance substantially across both single- and multi-hop document question answering, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. Our method can be further adapted into an efficient sparse variant, yielding near-constant encoding cost with respect to context length while preserving (and sometimes improving) performance. We also present simple theoretical arguments that illustrate why souping works and when it may fail, and discuss informally the advantages of weighted souping. Weighted state souping thus combines reusable context representations with selective retrieval, offering an efficient approach to language modeling over large collections of documents, tools, and other forms of structured context that increasingly dominate modern agentic workloads. † Harvard University ** Work done while at Apple Related readings and updates. item.title: Meta Releases Muse Ember, a 1M-Context Model for High-Volume Agent Work
item.abstract: Meta Superintelligence Labs has released Muse Ember , its smallest and most efficient model. Meta Muse Ember is a hosted multimodal reasoning model built for the repetitive steps inside agents. Meta lists tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction and long document parsing as targets. It scores 36 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, level with Claude Haiku 5.5 at max effort. Meta puts its cost at about $0.14 per index task. Muse Ember is a small reasoning model from Meta for high-volume agent subtasks. It is the fourth model under the Muse brand , after Spark, Glimmer and Wonder. Meta positions it below its larger models. Muse Wonder handles the hardest problems and Muse Spark covers coding and agentic workflows. Ember takes repeatable coding and agent tasks at scale. Meta’s own framing: Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume. Muse Ember is the first model Meta trained using Muse Wonder Full, its largest model. The model natively accepts text, images, audio and video. That lets an agent read screenshots, charts, scanned pages, voice memos and meeting recordings without a separate model. It also operates desktop apps from screenshots. The 1M-token context window fits a full codebase or document set in one call. Output runs up to 512K tokens, 4x the 128K cap on both rivals. All results below are at max reasoning effort, as reported by Meta. Some come from Artificial Analysis (AA), others from Meta’s internal suite. Muse Ember costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens . Cached input costs $0.004 per million. Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna list the same base rates. item.title: My AI agents found an unmapped Maya site
item.abstract:
My AI Agents (Re)discovered a Maya Site in 72 Hours 5 min read (Last edit: 11 Nov) Update (11 November): it turns out the site had already been mapped in Estrada-Belli et al. 2025 . The agents missed it while going through the literature, so they rediscovered it rather than discovered it (it just wasn't in the register of Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History, INAH, yet). Still work to do then! The rest of the story still holds. By analyzing NASA lidar data, my AI agents found a Maya site in Mexico that wasn't in the official register. (It turned out archaeologists had mapped it already, more on that at the end.) It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive. Lidar: bare ground, 2013 Satellite image today Drag the slider. The same hilltop today from a satellite (just trees) and in lidar (no trees). Colours show height. Satellite © Esri, Maxar, Earthstar Geographics. Disclaimer: I'm not an archaeologist. I'm going to tell this story as a diary, because the timeline is probably the best part. 18 October I was traveling in Peru, Gemini-ing about the history of the place, when I learned about Hiram Bingham , the American explorer who "discovered" Machu Picchu in 1911. "What luck!" I thought. He was actually looking for a different city, Vilcabamba , the last refuge of the Incas, when a local farmer in the valley below guided him to the ruins. "Imagine if Bingham had our tools," I thought. "What would he do?" Left: Bingham at his tent, 1912. Right: Machu Picchu, photographed by Bingham the same year. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons ( left , right ). I brainstormed a bit with a few agents (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok), and they all said lidar . From above, a ruin in the jungle is just a bunch of trees (like Machu Picchu before it was cleared), so satellite photos don't help much. Lidar, instead, fires laser pulses through the gaps in the canopy and maps the ground underneath. [1] So the agents went looking for lidar data. Peru isn't well covered, and hiring a company to do a survey meant permits, costs and bureaucracy, so I gave up on that. Then I thought: why not the Maya ? Their region is much better covered by public lidar. That night, I asked the agents to analyze it and went to bed. 19 October I woke up and checked the agents' reports. 'DAMN!' They had found lots of villages and other regular shapes that looked like structures or houses. A few of the sites the agents flagged overnight. Keep an eye on the bottom-left one. So how did they do it? They turned the lidar strips (about 1,200 km² of jungle) into images, and 48 agents went through them one by one like very patient archaeologists, looking for pyramids, platforms, and plazas while filtering out natural hills, sinkholes, and roads. There was no special model or classifier involved: the agents literally looked at the pictures, following a precise guide. Me: That's awesome! Please check which of these villages haven't been discovered yet. Search both the literature and the archives. …a few hours later… Agent: One major village doesn't seem to have been registered. This is the hilltop from the top of this post. It sits on the edge of a cliff, under the jungle, and it has straight edges and sharp corners. Nature doesn't really do straight lines. Zooming in, there's a levelled plaza, an oval pyramid at least 8–12 m tall, a raised courtyard attached to it and a flat-bottomed hollow that might have been a water reservoir. The hilltop with the trees removed (top), and a zoom into its civic centre (bottom). And this is what it looks like in 3D. The site in 3D, from the lidar. Heights exaggerated ~1.5×. Me: OK, what should I do? Agent: You should contact INAH (Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History), write a report on your discovery, and check whether the site is in their register. Sometimes they have unpublished results. Me: OK, how do I contact INAH? How does the reporting process work? Agent: …instructions for the report… + email addresses Me: OK, please do the report. And I went to bed. 20 October I iterated on the report a bit, since a few things were off, and translated it into Spanish to improve the chances of getting a reply (at least, that's what Claude suggested). I don't speak Spanish, so I had to trust the agents on that one. The agents also checked the raw point cloud, to make sure the shapes were really on the ground and not created by the trees. Green dots are leaves, brown dots are the ground. Two slices through the raw lidar points. Under 10–17 m of forest, the ground (brown) traces the plaza, the pyramid and the courtyard. Then I sent the report to INAH. The top of my letter to INAH. The exact coordinates went in a confidential annex, not shown here. 21 October INAH replied: they checked their records and found no registered archaeological site at that location . INAH's reply. The highlighted part: "…no registered archaeological site was identified at the location given in your report." At that point I thought nobody had put it on a map before. I was wrong (see below). So what was it? This part is speculation, from a long chat with the agents. It looks like a small Maya civic centre from the Classic period (roughly AD 250–900), basically the "downtown" of a local elite. The plaza is where people gathered, for ceremonies and maybe even a market. The pyramid was probably a temple, and the raised courtyard next to it might have been where the local ruler lived. The hollow could have been an aguada , a rainwater reservoir: Maya towns needed them to get through the dry season. Or it's just a hole. The three platforms around were probably houses. I asked Gemini to imagine how it looked back then: How it might have looked around AD 700. Generated with Gemini from the lidar layout For similar studies, have a look at how NASA's G-LiHT instrument works ( Cook et al. 2013 ) and how lidar collected for environmental research can be reused for archaeology ( Golden et al. 2016 ). In 2024, archaeologists found a whole Maya city in Mexico this way ( Auld-Thomas et al. 2024 ), others mapped settlements across the Maya lowlands, including this very site ( Estrada-Belli et al. 2025 ), and another study found what may have been ancient Maya marketplaces ( Šprajc 2026 ). What's next The site is now in the hands of the people who should have it: Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) and the archaeologists who mapped it first. If anything comes out of it, I'll post an update. What I've learned You can just do things. I'm not an archaeologist, so I didn't know this was supposed to be hard. I just picked an old problem, tried the most obvious thing and threw some compute at it. Being a naive outsider might be a superpower now. And it turned out professional archaeologists had already mapped the same site. I guess that's a good sign: an outsider with agents ended up in a similar place to the experts. And I don't think this is really about archaeology. So far, most agentic AI stories have been about coding, math and physics, but it's much more general than that, and I hope this small example makes it a bit more obvious. We are on the brink of a revolution in all the sciences, and the only bottlenecks left will be curiosity and imagination (and compute). At this point, we should probably lidar the whole planet and let the agents discover the rest. If you don't know how lidar works, copy and paste this prompt into your favorite AI tool: "Build an HTML page that explains how lidar works, with beautiful visualizations." ↩

item.title: UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents
item.abstract: Teams building AI agents on AWS use a range of frameworks, including LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Each framework records agent execution in its own way, so the structure of messages, tool calls, and handoffs between agents differs from one to the next. Evaluation tooling tends to follow the same boundaries: teams build metrics, scoring logic, and result storage against a single framework’s trace format, and they must rebuild them when they switch frameworks or run agents on more than one. This coupling makes a basic development question harder to answer: did a change to the prompt, model, or tools improve the agent? Answering it requires consistent metrics across versions of an agent and a shared record of past results to compare against. Agent quality also spans several dimensions that a single accuracy score does not capture: tool calling, response quality, responsible AI, performance, multi-turn conversation, multi-agent coordination, and reasoning. In this post, we introduce the Universal Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF). Customers across 12 organizations in the telecom, healthcare, and financial services industries used UAEF to evaluate their AI agents with one consistent set of metrics and compare agent versions before release. UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system: it uses adapters to convert traces from each framework into a common format, then scores those traces with 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions. It stores the results in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and generates reports and insights that inform the next iteration of the agent. This post describes how UAEF works, provides a playbook for choosing metrics and preparing datasets, and points to runnable notebooks for each supported framework. UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system for AI agents. It takes the agent a team already has and scores it the same way across supported frameworks and runtimes. UAEF takes two inputs: the agent under test and a dataset to run it on. The dataset provides the inputs for each test case, and it can also include ground-truth answers, the expected output for each input. Ground truth is optional, and only metrics that compare the agent’s response against a reference use it. To evaluate tool calling, the ground truth must also include the expected tool calls for each test case: which tools the agent should call, in what order, and with what arguments. Everything after that happens inside the UAEF. Figure 1 shows the path a single evaluation takes, from the inputs to the reports and insights. First, an adapter reads the agent’s native execution, its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs, and normalizes it into one canonical trace, so that the steps that follow are identical no matter which framework produced the agent. Next, UAEF screens the trace for personally identifiable information (PII), such as email addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers, before data is stored. The evaluation engine then scores the trace on a selection from 36 built-in metrics across 7 quality dimensions. When you persist a run, UAEF records it as an experiment in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3: Amazon DynamoDB holds the per-experiment metadata used for listing and comparison, and Amazon S3 holds the full results. With runs stored, a team can compare an agent version against a baseline to detect regressions and generate reports and insights that explain what changed and why. Those reports close the loop: the team evaluates the agent, learns what regressed or improved, changes the prompt, model, or tools, and evaluates again. Figure 1: UAEF closed-loop evaluation data flow The rest of this section follows that flow in order: the adapters that make UAEF framework-agnostic, the evaluation engine and its metrics, PII detection, experiment storage and comparison, and the reports that close the loop. Adapters are what make UAEF framework-agnostic. An adapter reads the record of an agent’s run, including its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs. It converts that record into one canonical representation called the AgentTrace , which is the only thing the rest of UAEF scores. Because of that conversion, UAEF works with the agent, whatever SDK it was built with (such as LangGraph, LangChain, or Strands Agents). It can run locally, behind an HTTP endpoint, or on a managed runtime such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with traces in Langfuse or not captured at all. UAEF provides an adapter for each of these, and they produce the same AgentTrace , so metrics, scores, and comparisons stay consistent across every one of them. A trace reaches UAEF two ways. If one already exists, from a past run, a log, or an observability store, it is handed to UAEF and the matching adapter normalizes it. If not, UAEF invokes the agent for you: given a runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) or an HTTP endpoint, it calls the agent on each dataset input, collects the response, and adapts it in one step. Either way, the output is the same AgentTrace . Because every metric, mode, and report operates on the AgentTrace rather than on a framework native format, the scoring that follows is identical no matter where the trace came from. That separation, normalization first and scoring second, is what lets a team compare an agent built on one framework against an agent built on another on a single scale. The evaluation engine scores a canonical trace across 7 quality dimensions, each capturing a distinct aspect of agent behavior that a single accuracy number would hide. Tool calling measures whether the agent selected the right tools, called them in a sensible order, and passed valid arguments. Response quality measures whether the final answer is relevant, complete, accurate, and grounded in the provided context rather than hallucinated. Responsible AI measures safety, bias, toxicity, and resistance to prompt injection. Performance measures operational cost in latency, token use, and throughput. Multi-turn measures how well the agent sustains a conversation, including context retention, coherence, and goal completion across turns. Multi-agent measures coordination in systems of cooperating agents, such as task delegation and the division of work. Reasoning measures the internal logic of the agent’s chain of thought, including consistency and freedom from fallacies. Each dimension is computed by one or more of 36 built-in metrics, and every metric returns a normalized score in the interval [0, 1], where 1 is best, so dimensions and the overall result share one scale. Metrics come in two families. Deterministic metrics compute a score directly from the trace and the ground truth and reproduce exactly on repeated runs. Large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge metrics score qualities that resist a closed-form definition, such as response relevance or safety, by prompting a judge model on Amazon Bedrock. You can also add your own custom metrics or draw on the RAGAS and DeepEval integrations. Because judge metrics feed an agent’s own output back into a prompt, that content is treated as untrusted input: an agent that can influence its judge can influence its own scores. The rubric is sent separately from the content, and the content is escaped so it cannot break out of its delimiter and be read as instructions. Each judge response is parsed strictly and must cite a verbatim span of the content it scored. A score whose evidence is not found is rejected rather than recorded. Judge scores are evaluation signal, not a safety decision, and should not gate a security control. For runtime enforcement on the agent itself, apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails in its own invocation path. The full model is in SECURITY.md. UAEF records each evaluation as an experiment, so results from different agent versions can be compared later.
