item.title: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model
item.abstract: Back to Articles BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model Team Article Published November 11, 2026 Upvote 16 +10 Milan Gritta milangritta Follow qvac Jihye Back happy-jihye Follow qvac JinUk, Cho jucho2725 Follow qvac ohjoon kwon joooon Follow qvac Patrik Lambert patrik-lambert Follow qvac Mathias Buus mafintosh Follow qvac Amril Nurman Nurman Follow qvac Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models. Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information. 🤗 Model (safetensors) | 📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4) Figure 1: BotPsy-0.8B significantly outperforms its base model and leads five of the six tool-use and agentic benchmarks, including against Qwen3.5-2B-Think (2.5× its size); only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think edge ahead. Figure 2: Knowledge: tool-use training preserved and improved BotPsy's general knowledge compared to similarly sized models, though overall knowledge still scales primarily with parameter count. Instruction following: BotPsy excels at following explicit instructions and multi-turn tasks, though its performance drops as instructions accumulate and lags in lower-resource languages. Copyright Complaints We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement. Key Highlights Benchmark results Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think on key benchmarks: BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5 (mean of the retail, telecom and banking subsets). Best agent in its category: BotPsy outperforms leading models in the ≤1.2B-parameter weight class (Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think, LFM2.5-1.2B-Think, MiniCPM5-1B-Think) on all six tool-use and agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, Claw-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus. Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5). Model capabilities More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9). Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model. Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested. Safety, efficiency and deployment Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%. More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device. Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp. Broader Vision Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware.

item.title: Using mathematics to validate network configurations
item.abstract: Corporations, banks, hospitals, and academic institutions all rely on wide-area networks (WANs) to connect their local networks across geographic regions. Within a WAN, however, it’s often necessary to isolate different computational resources from each other: for example, coding environments used to test new website features should remain separate from active websites. Customers rely on such isolation — or segmentation — to help protect sensitive data; a single misconfiguration of segmentation rules could allow traffic to reach unintended parts of a network or allow data to cross organizational boundaries. Historically, validating network segmentation has involved mapping the network by sending packets through it. The size and complexity of modern networks, however, make it impractical to build a complete map this way, so organizations instead rely on a sampling process that sends packets through only portions of the network. The result is that network segmentation is rarely validated exhaustively. By using Tiros, Amazon Web Services’ automated-reasoning tool for analyzing network connectivity, we’re offering an alternative to dynamic sampling that is designed to validate segmentation across all modeled paths. Previously, Tiros had been used in customer-facing services such as Amazon Inspector, VPC Reachability Analyzer, and Network Access Analyzer. These services focus on reachability, or determining whether some sequence of valid requests leads from one network resource to another. Our key insight is that if we can determine the reachable paths in a network, then we can also identify the absence of paths between particular resources. Fundamentally, automated segmentation validation is a static process: it examines a network without relying on dynamic packet traffic. Using Tiros, we can analyze the topology of a deployed network as frequently as every hour. These analyses provide a mathematical demonstration that the topological description aligns with our isolation specifications. Automated segmentation validation In modern networking, a virtual network sits on top of the physical network of servers and wires and other components. Segmentation is achieved through logical rules and routing policies rather than physical isolation of network hardware. We consider the case in which an Amazon Web Services (AWS) customer is using the AWS Cloud WAN service to configure and deploy a large organizational WAN. To validate network segmentation using Tiros, we first collect the customer’s Cloud WAN configuration from route tables, “attachments” (which are like a virtual cable within the network), and policy documents. Specialized software converts these configurations into logical propositions that describe network behavior. Now, we have a configuration that’s expressed logically, so that automated reasoning tools can analyze it. Then we ask Tiros, “Which attachments can reach which attachments with which destination IPs?” Tiros generates the satisfying assignments it can derive from the network description, each of which corresponds to a path. Our system checks that no path exists between segments that the policy declares should be off limits from each other. If actual reachability matches the expected segmentation, the validation check succeeds; if they differ, the system alerts an operator. Virtual private clouds and network predicates Consider a global company that uses Cloud WAN to connect resources all over the world and manage a website for selling and supporting its products. When the company updates its website, it does so from a replica of the public-facing website inside the development environment within Cloud WAN. The production environment needs to be strictly contained, so that tests and changes not yet ready for deployment don’t reach the live website, which is maintained in the separate production environment. So the company’s software developers write a policy, or a collection of logical rules, that captures the need for this segmentation. The policy defines two segments, production and development, across two regions, us-east-1 and us-west-2, as in the figure above. Attachment policies use tags to assign Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs, logically separated networks within larger networks) to various other network segments. In this policy, VPCs are tagged such that VPC-prod-use1 and VPC-prod-usw2 join the production segment and VPC-dev-use1 joins the development segment, as in the figure. Observe, also, that in the figure, VPC-prod-use1 and VPC-dev-use1 are destinations within the same address space, 10.0.0.0/16. In this context, segmentation becomes critical; if the VPCs were deployed within the same segment, or segmentation was misconfigured, a packet destined for that address space would have a nondeterministic destination, VPC-prod-use1 or VPC-dev-use1. Practically speaking, such a misconfiguration could cause customer traffic to erroneously arrive in a development VPC. Using Tiros, we take the core network configuration above and build a logical model of the network composed of rules (conditional predicates) and facts (unconditional predicates). Once the model is built, we can query Tiros for the instances of segmentation it derives for the attachments in the model. When given predicates, facts, and a query, Tiros generates the assignments associated with each VPC and IP for which the query is provable within the model. If, for instance, Tiros finds no assignment where a production VPC reaches a development VPC, or a development VPC reaches a production VPC, then the results indicate that the core network’s segmentation aligns with the stated policy. Future work Segmentation validation demonstrates how automated reasoning can provide the kind of assurance that packet-based testing cannot. By encoding network configurations as logical propositions and using Tiros to explore the possible paths in the model, we can check segmentation against the stated policy rather than just sampling it. Customers do not need to run separate reachability tests. This approach is not unique to Cloud WAN. Across AWS, automated reasoning is used to analyze properties of systems that are too large to test exhaustively. Using an engine called Zelkova, IAM Access Analyzer helps you identify whether a policy could grant access to a resource from outside your account and uses the same reasoning to help identify S3 buckets that are shared publicly or with other accounts. Similarly, VPC Reachability Analyzer helps determine whether one resource can reach another in your network. They all share the same foundation: translating configurations into logic and checking whether the properties you care about hold.

item.title: Running AV Reasoning Models Within Onboard Compute and Latency Limits
item.abstract:
Autonomous vehicle (AV) developers need reasoning models that can operate within the compute and latency constraints of an onboard system. Larger models provide a foundation for developing these capabilities, but moving them into a vehicle requires additional work to reduce model size, preserve useful reasoning, and validate performance on the target hardware. NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Edge addresses this need with an adaptive reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) model designed for real-time operation on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor . Built on the 2B Nemotron-based reasoning backbone of NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge and paired with a diffusion action expert, it leverages surround-camera observations, temporal context, and navigation inputs to generate Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning and future driving trajectories. It reasons adaptively , generating reasoning only when needed, reducing unnecessary token generation and conserving inference compute during routine driving. Alpamayo 2 Edge is post-trained with closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL) in NVIDIA AlpaGym , improving closed-loop driving performance by 48.9% on top of the best-performing checkpoint without closed-loop RL. Together, these capabilities give developers a strong, edge-ready foundation for bringing reasoning-based driving into an onboard stack. Making a reasoning model compact enough for onboard deployment introduces a key challenge: preserving the quality of its reasoning and driving behavior as model size is reduced. This requires a way to measure reasoning quality and use that feedback to improve the model. NVIDIA AlpaJudge is the human-calibrated evaluation and reward model used in Alpamayo 2 Edge development to evaluate reasoning traces, select higher-value training data, and provide RL rewards. This post introduces Alpamayo 2 Edge, explains its inference optimization on DRIVE AGX Thor, and explores three ways to use AlpaJudge in AV development workflows: Run AlpaJudge-RB and AlpaJudge-RF on a PhysicalAI-AV sample, inspect their scores, and adapt the evaluation to policy-generated reasoning Select training examples that expose useful learning opportunities Use human-aligned reasoning scores as rewards for post-training Together, these workflows connect an edge-oriented driving model with a repeatable process for measuring and improving it. Bring reasoning-based driving to the edge An onboard driving model must interpret a changing scene and produce a useful trajectory within the system’s inference budget. The key question is how much driving and reasoning capability a model retains under that constraint. Figure 1. Alpamayo 2 Edge processes multi-camera video, ego-motion history, and navigation instructions to generate adaptive causal reasoning and driving trajectories, with support for optional visual question answering To balance model capacity and efficiency, Alpamayo 2 Edge leverages multiple new features: A 2B-parameter Nemotron-based reasoning backbone, sized for onboard inference Adaptive reasoning, reducing unnecessary token generation and conserving inference compute during routine driving Offline distillation, training with CoC reasoning autolabels generated by Alpamayo 2 Super Closed-loop reinforcement learning post-training in AlpaGym , in which the model learns from the consequences of its actions end-to-end in simulation Multi-resolution inputs to efficiently encode surround-view observations online Speculative decoding with DFlash2 to accelerate online reasoning without sacrificing quality Recipes for quantization and inference acceleration with NVIDIA TensorRT and NVIDIA TensorRT-Edge-LLM Figure 2, below, shows how these choices translate into capability, comparing Alpamayo 2 Edge with Qwen-Drive-1.0 across closed-loop driving, open-loop trajectory prediction, and scene understanding and reasoning. Figure 2. Alpamayo 2 Edge (2B) compared with Qwen-Drive-1.0 (4B) across closed-loop driving, open-loop driving, and scene understanding and reasoning benchmarks. Of note, Alpamayo 2 Edge achieves approximately 60× the distance between at-fault incidents in AlpaSim Early partner feedback also highlights Alpamayo 2 Edge’s driving performance and inference speed: “Within days of getting early access to Alpamayo 2 Edge, we had it running closed-loop in NuRec reconstructions of our own London street recordings. In our early simulation tests, Edge kept its lane in more than twice as many runs as Alpamayo 1.5, recovered from lane offsets about 40% more often, and out of the box planned roughly twice as fast as our hand-tuned Alpamayo 1.5 server on the same GPU.” — Matas Simonavicius, CTO, PORT “Alpamayo 2 Edge demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities, reducing displacement error (minADE) by 13.6% and lateral prediction error (RMSE) at 3 seconds by 46.1% compared to Alpamayo 2 Super in our zero-shot evaluation, despite substantial differences in sensor configurations. Fine-tuning on our own driving data delivered a further 44.2% reduction in displacement error compared to the Alpamayo 2 Edge baseline. Within just a few days, we went from receiving the model to running our first tests on a real vehicle.” — Luca Crotti, co-founder and motion planning lead, Niulinx Video 1. Niulinx’s driving demonstration shows the vehicle stopping for a traffic officer’s signal and yielding to pedestrians at a crosswalk “In less than 48 hours, we made NVIDIA’s Alpamayo 2 Edge run at 10 Hz on AGX Thor for real-time planning.”— Hans Salomonsson, CEO and co-founder, Embedl Video 2.
